books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, A. Slavery and the Southern “Way of Life”

primary_sources: John C. Calhoun, "Slavery a Positive Good," Senate speech, February 6, 1837

stimulus.text:
John C. Calhoun, senator from South Carolina, speaking in the Senate on February 6, 1837, during debate over abolitionist petitions:

“But let me not be understood as admitting, even by implication, that the existing relations between the two races in the slaveholding States is an evil:—far otherwise; I hold it to be a good, as it has thus far proved itself to be to both, and will continue to prove so if not disturbed by the fell spirit of abolition.”

“I fearlessly assert that the existing relation between the two races in the South, against which these blind fanatics are waging war, forms the most solid and durable foundation on which to rear free and stable political institutions.”
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from John C. Calhoun, Senate speech, February 6, 1837, as printed on Wikisource (Slavery a Positive Good). Viewed and checked before writing.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from John C. Calhoun, Senate speech, February 6, 1837, public domain
stem: Calhoun gave this speech during a Senate debate over abolitionist petitions. That situation best explains why he did what?

options.text: Defended slavery openly before a national audience
Asked the Senate to ban abolitionist newspapers in the South
options.misconception: Calhoun argued against receiving the petitions; he did not ask to ban Southern newspapers.

options.text: Proposed that the Senate buy enslaved people and free them
options.misconception: Calhoun defended slavery; buying and freeing enslaved people is the opposite of his argument.

options.text: Urged Southern states to leave the Union at once
options.misconception: Calhoun warned about the Union, but in 1837 he did not urge immediate secession.

rationales.A: Abolitionist petitions put slavery on the Senate floor, and Calhoun answered by calling slavery a positive good, not a necessary evil.
rationales.B: Calhoun argued against receiving the petitions. He did not ask to ban Southern newspapers.
rationales.C: Calhoun defended slavery. Buying and freeing enslaved people is the opposite of his argument.
rationales.D: Calhoun warned about the Union, but in 1837 he did not urge immediate secession.
rationales.general:
1. Name the occasion. Abolitionist petitions reached the Senate, and Calhoun rose to answer them.
2. Ask what the occasion forced. He had to defend slavery before a national audience, not just to Southern voters.
3. Read the tone. He refuses to admit slavery is an evil and calls it a good, which is an open defense, not an apology.
Background: Earlier Southerners had often called slavery a necessary evil; Calhoun broke with that language in this speech.
Remember: the occasion of a speech often explains its boldness.
